title: The problem of evil
examples: What is the problem of evil?
If God is good, why is there suffering?

explain.say: Many religions believe in a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing and all-good. Yet the world contains terrible suffering. How can both be true? That puzzle is called the problem of evil.

An old version is often credited to the Greek philosopher Epicurus. If God wants to stop evil but can't, God is not all-powerful. If God can but won't, God is not all-good. If God is both, why is there evil?

items: All-good: God would want to stop it

explain.say: Philosophers separate two kinds of evil. Moral evil is harm people cause by their choices, like cruelty or war. Natural evil is suffering from nature, like earthquakes and disease, which no person chose.

Believers have offered answers called theodicies. Augustine said evil is not a thing God made but the loss of good, which entered through the misuse of free will. Irenaeus said the world is a place where souls grow, and facing hardship helps people become good.

a: Evil is a lack of good
It came from misused free will

draw.text: Free will defence: a world of free people, able to choose good, is worth the risk of evil.

explain.say: Other traditions answer differently. Hindus and Buddhists often explain suffering through karma across many lives, and Buddhism focuses on ending suffering. The Book of Job wrestles with innocent suffering, and the Qur'an describes hardships as a test of patience and faith.

items: Hinduism | Karma: actions shape this and future lives
Buddhism | Suffering, dukkha, can be ended on the Eightfold Path
Judaism | Job: trust, even without full answers
Christianity | God shares suffering in Jesus on the cross
Islam | Hardship as a test; patience, sabr

explain.say: Critics reply that some suffering is so great, or falls on such innocent beings like children and animals, that no answer explains it. Some find this a reason not to believe; many believers keep their faith while still asking why. The debate remains open.

items: Why so much suffering, not just some?
Why do children and animals suffer?
Natural evil is not caused by free will
Faith may trust without a full answer

faq.q: What is the problem of evil?
faq.a: The problem of evil asks how an all-powerful, all-knowing and all-good God could allow evil and suffering. If God could stop it and wanted to, why does it exist? It is one of the oldest and most discussed questions in philosophy of religion.
asks: what is the problem of suffering

faq.q: If God is good, why is there suffering?
faq.a: Believers give several answers. Some say suffering comes from people misusing their free will; others that hardship helps us grow in courage and compassion; others trust that God has reasons we cannot see. Critics say these answers do not explain the amount of suffering. People weigh these responses differently.
asks: why do bad things happen to good people
why would a good God let people suffer

faq.a: A theodicy is an attempt to explain why a good and all-powerful God allows evil. The word was coined by the philosopher Leibniz in 1710, from Greek words meaning God and justice. Famous theodicies come from Augustine and Irenaeus.

faq.q: What is the difference between moral evil and natural evil?
faq.a: Moral evil is suffering caused by people's choices, such as cruelty, theft or war. Natural evil is suffering caused by nature, such as earthquakes, floods and disease. Natural evil is often seen as harder for believers to explain, since no human chose it.

Augustine, a Christian thinker of the 4th and 5th centuries, taught that God created a perfect world, and evil is not a thing in itself but a lack or loss of good. Evil entered when angels and humans misused their free will, and natural evil followed from that fall.

Irenaeus, a 2nd-century Christian bishop, suggested humans were created immature and must grow towards goodness. The modern philosopher John Hick developed this as soul-making: a world with real challenges lets people freely develop virtues like courage, patience and compassion.

faq.q: What is the free will defence?
faq.a: The free will defence says that a world with free people, who can truly choose to love and do good, is more valuable than a world of puppets. But real freedom means people can also choose evil. The philosopher Alvin Plantinga gave a well-known modern version.
asks: why doesn't God stop evil people

faq.q: Who first asked the problem of evil?
faq.a: The question is ancient. A famous version is often credited to the Greek philosopher Epicurus, around 300 BCE, though it comes to us through later writers. The Book of Job in the Hebrew Bible also wrestles with why the innocent suffer.
asks: who came up with the problem of evil

faq.q: What does the Book of Job say about suffering?
faq.a: Job is a good man who loses his children, wealth and health. His friends insist he must have sinned, but Job protests his innocence and questions God. God answers from a whirlwind by showing the vastness of creation, rather than giving a simple explanation, and Job's fortunes are restored.

faq.q: How do Hindus and Buddhists explain suffering?
faq.a: Many Hindus and Buddhists explain suffering through karma: actions in this and earlier lives shape what happens to us, across a cycle of rebirth. Buddhism's first noble truth says life involves suffering, dukkha, and its path aims to end suffering rather than to explain a creator's choices.
asks: why do people suffer in Hinduism

faq.q: How does Islam respond to suffering?
faq.a: The Qur'an describes hardship as a test from God, to be met with patience, sabr, and trust. Muslims believe God is wise and merciful, that good people will be rewarded, and that all wrongs will be justly settled on the Day of Judgement.
asks: suffering as a test in Islam

faq.q: What is the evidential problem of evil?
faq.a: The logical problem claims God and evil cannot both exist. The evidential problem, argued by William Rowe, says something milder: the huge amount of seemingly pointless suffering, like an animal dying slowly in a forest fire, makes God's existence less likely. Believers reply that we may not see God's reasons.
asks: logical vs evidential problem of evil

faq.q: Does the problem of evil prove God doesn't exist?
faq.a: Philosophers disagree. Some, like J. L. Mackie, argued it shows belief in such a God is inconsistent; many others, like Alvin Plantinga, argued that God and evil can logically exist together. Many believers say it is a real mystery that tests faith but does not end it.
asks: is the problem of evil an argument against God
can God and evil both exist

faq.q: What is the best of all possible worlds?
faq.a: The philosopher Leibniz argued that God, being perfect, must have created the best world possible, even though it contains evil, because any other world would be worse overall. The writer Voltaire mocked this idea in his story Candide.

facts: The word theodicy was coined by Gottfried Leibniz in 1710.
Augustine described evil as a privation, a lack or loss of good.
Irenaeus's ideas were developed into the soul-making theodicy by the philosopher John Hick.
Moral evil is caused by human choices; natural evil comes from nature, like earthquakes and disease.
A famous form of the problem of evil is often credited to the Greek philosopher Epicurus.

quiz.show: An earthquake is an example of...
quiz.why: Natural evil is suffering caused by nature rather than human choice, like earthquakes, floods and disease.

wrong.0: Moral evil is caused by people's choices, such as cruelty or war.
wrong.2: Philosophers classify earthquake suffering as natural evil.

quiz.say: Apply. A believer says, facing hard times helped me become braver and more compassionate. Which theodicy does this fit best?
quiz.show: Hardship made me braver and kinder: which theodicy?
quiz.why: Irenaeus and later John Hick argued that the world is a place for soul-making, where challenges help people grow in virtue.

wrong.0: Augustine explains evil as a lack of good caused by misused free will, not as growth.
wrong.2: The design argument is an argument for God from order, not a response to evil.
wrong.3: Pascal's wager is about whether to believe, not about why suffering exists.

quiz.say: Think. Why do critics say the free will defence struggles with earthquakes and disease?
quiz.show: Why is natural evil hard for the free will defence?

options.show: Earthquakes are not caused by anyone's free choice
options.say: Earthquakes are not caused by anyone's free choice

quiz.why: The free will defence explains evil people choose, but natural disasters and disease seem to happen without anyone choosing them, so believers need further answers.

wrong.1: Earthquakes clearly do cause great suffering; that is why they raise the problem.
wrong.2: The defence assumes free will exists; the problem is that natural evil isn't caused by it.
